title: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Decree of Cyrus
summary: After Josiah's death, four kings follow in quick succession: Jehoahaz is deposed by Egypt, Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin are taken or threatened by Babylon, and Zedekiah rebels and refuses to humble himself before Jeremiah. Because the people and priests mock God's messengers, God brings Nebuchadnezzar, who kills, plunders, burns the temple, breaks down Jerusalem's wall, and carries the survivors to Babylon, while the land keeps its Sabbaths for seventy years. The book ends with Cyrus of Persia proclaiming that the LORD has appointed him to build God's house in Jerusalem and inviting God's people to go up.
story: This is the end of the story Chronicles has been telling since Adam in 1 Chronicles 1: the line of David, the temple, and the people gathered around it. In a few verses the kingdom that David founded and Solomon glorified collapses. The Chronicler does not linger on the details of the siege; he gives the reason, which he has taught in every reign: God sent messengers again and again because he had compassion, and they mocked them until there was no remedy. Yet the book does not end in ruins. Its final words are a door opening: a pagan king, moved by the LORD, invites the exiles to go up and rebuild. In the traditional Hebrew order, Chronicles is the last book of the Bible, so the Hebrew Scriptures close on that invitation.
historical:
The chapter covers about seventy years in outline. Jehoahaz reigned three months in 609 BC before Neco of Egypt removed him. Jehoiakim, Neco's appointee, ruled about 609 to 598 BC and became Babylon's vassal after Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC. His son Jehoiachin reigned three months before surrendering to Nebuchadnezzar; the Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform record of the empire's years, dates Jerusalem's capture to early 597 BC. Babylonian administrative tablets later list food rations for Jehoiachin, king of Judah, in Babylon. Zedekiah, placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar, rebelled, and Jerusalem fell after a long siege in 587 or 586 BC; the temple was burned. The fuller accounts are in 2 Kings 23:31 to 25:30 and Jeremiah 39 and 52.

Verse 6 says Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim to take him to Babylon, while 2 Kings 24:6 says he died in Jerusalem, and whether he was actually deported is uncertain. Babylon fell to Cyrus the Persian in 539 BC, and in his first year as ruler of Babylon (539/538 BC) he issued the decree quoted at the end of the chapter and at the start of Ezra (Ezra 1:1-3). The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay inscription now in the British Museum, records Cyrus's policy of returning displaced peoples and their gods to their homelands, though it does not mention Judah.
cultural:
Conquerors in this era changed the names of vassal kings (verse 4) as a sign of their authority, imposed tribute, and carried off temple treasures to their own gods' temples as trophies (verse 7). Deporting a nation's leaders, craftsmen, and elite was standard Babylonian policy for crushing rebellion, and the Chaldeans were the people whose dynasty ruled Babylon at this time.

The mention of the land's Sabbaths (verse 21) draws on the Law's command that the land rest every seventh year (Leviticus 25:1-7) and its warning that if Israel refused, the land would enjoy its Sabbaths while the people were in exile (Leviticus 26:34-35). The seventy years come from Jeremiah's prophecy (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10). The Chronicler combines Leviticus and Jeremiah to read the exile as both judgment and a kind of forced rest, a desolation that also prepared for renewal. Cyrus's calling the LORD “the God of heaven” fits the respectful language Persian rulers used toward the gods of their subject peoples.
literary: The chapter moves at speed. The four kings are covered in formulaic paragraphs, each shorter than any earlier reign, as though the story is running out of breath. Then comes the Chronicler's theological summary (verses 14-16), one of the most important passages in the book: the LORD sent his messengers “again and again” because he “had compassion” on his people, but they mocked, despised, and scoffed until the wrath of the LORD was stirred “beyond remedy.” The word for having compassion in verse 15 returns in verse 17 in the negative, as the Babylonians show no pity. The final two verses mirror each other: Jeremiah's word is fulfilled in the desolation (verse 21) and again in the decree (verse 22). The book's last word in Hebrew means and let him go up, an ending that points forward rather than closing the story.

outline.t: Zedekiah's rebellion and the people's mocking of the prophets

doctrines.note: The fall of Jerusalem is presented as God's judgment after long patience. Judgment comes only when warnings sent out of compassion have been refused until there was no remedy.
God gives Judah into Nebuchadnezzar's hand and stirs the spirit of Cyrus. The great empires of the age act freely, yet within God's purposes for his people.

The book ends not with ruins but with a decree to rebuild and an invitation to go up. The exile is real judgment, but it is not the end; God's word through Jeremiah promised both the desolation and the return.

words.note: Chamal, to have compassion or spare. In verse 15 God sends his messengers because he had compassion on his people; in verse 17 the Babylonians spare no one. The repeated word shows that God's mercy, once refused, was replaced by an enemy without mercy.

Marpe, healing or remedy. The wrath rose until there was no healing (verse 16). The word recalls God's promise to heal the land of a humble people (7:14); by the end, the people had closed the door that promise held open.

Shabbat, Sabbath or rest. The land enjoyed its Sabbaths during the desolation (verse 21). The word turns the exile into a theological statement: the rest Israel had refused to give the land, God gave it anyway.

Ur, to rouse or stir up. The LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus (verse 22), the same language Chronicles uses when God stirs up foreign kings against Israel (1 Chronicles 5:26). Now he stirs a foreign king for his people's good.

christ: Matthew's genealogy of Jesus treats the deportation to Babylon as one of the three great turning points in Israel's history, alongside Abraham and David, and names Jechoniah (Jehoiachin) in the line that leads to Jesus (Matthew 1:11-12, 17). The line of David survived the exile, just as God had promised. The destroyed temple and the call to rebuild also prepare for Jesus' words about the temple of his body: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19-21). And the book's last word, go up, finds an echo in the Gospels' account of Jesus setting his face to go up to Jerusalem, where he would die and rise. These connections are the New Testament's own, and they show why the church reads the end of Chronicles as an open door rather than a closed book.

hard.q: How do the seventy years of exile add up?
hard.a: Jeremiah prophesied seventy years for Babylon's dominance (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10), and the Chronicler applies the number to the land's desolation. Interpreters count it in different ways. Some measure from Nebuchadnezzar's first move against Jerusalem around 605 BC to Cyrus's decree in 539/538 BC, roughly seventy years. Others count from the temple's destruction in 587 or 586 BC to its rebuilding, completed around 516 BC, also about seventy years. Others take seventy as a round number meaning a full lifetime, the complete span of a judgment (compare Psalm 90:10 and Isaiah 23:15). Each approach takes the prophecy seriously; they differ over whether it was meant as an exact count or a symbolic whole.

questions: Verse 15 says God kept sending messengers because he had compassion. How does it change your view of warnings to see them as acts of mercy?
The Hebrew Scriptures end with an invitation to go up and rebuild. What in your life needs rebuilding after a season of loss or failure?
God used both Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus for his purposes. How do you understand God's work through rulers and nations who do not know him?
